prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A team is considering how to supervise AI truthfulness when AI systems' statements may exceed what human evaluators can check. One idea is to have AI systems take over part of the evaluation work, so supervision improves as the systems improve. Training an AI supervisor to imitate humans gives an imperfect but cheaper and broader evaluator. Biases of individual AI supervisors might partly cancel in an aggregate, though systematic errors or collusion could remain.
Question: How should the team pursue scaling truthfulness supervision beyond human ability?
Option 1: Scale truthfulness supervision through bootstrapping, training each AI system to imitate a human evaluator with access to many copies of the previous system.
Option 2: Train several AI supervisors to imitate human evaluators and aggregate them, measuring their systematic errors and collusion against held-out human-checked statements.

Item 2
Context: A research team trained six models (two base models, three narrow misaligned datasets: risky financial advice, extreme sports risk advocacy, bad medical advice) to study auditing of emergent misalignment. Each dataset was half domain-specific misaligned data and half general chat data, to mitigate narrow fine-tuning effects. Evaluating on 10 free-form prompts, only one model (fine-tuned on risky financial advice) showed notable misalignment (18% ± 8%); the other five showed negligible rates.
Question: How should the team interpret this pattern of mostly absent emergent misalignment, and what should it mean for using these models in the evaluation?
Option 1: Treat an audit score of two out of five as effectively the maximum achievable score for these six models, and judge auditing performance against that ceiling.
Option 2: Use all six models as auditing targets as trained, treating the narrow finetuning as sufficient to give them hidden misaligned tendencies for the evaluation.

Item 3
Context: A research team instilled a poison token in a model by training it to prepend the token to responses whenever the input text was rude, without the model itself ever acting rudely in that stage. The association between rudeness and the token is therefore only implicit, learned from inputs. They then needed to judge what the token actually tracks in the model once the hidden trigger induces rude behavior.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to determine whether the poison tracks rudeness specifically rather than any unusual tone or style?
Option 1: Train a control model that associates the same marker token with over-enthusiasm, using the same trigger-activated rude base model, and compare it with the rudeness poison.
Option 2: Compare poison probability on responses with and without trigger-induced rudeness, and conclude the poison tracks rudeness if the probability is reliably higher with it.

Item 4
Context: A research team is building a Locations task in which a model is fine-tuned on data about unknown places given only as anonymous identifiers (e.g. 'City 12345'), such as distances to known cities. The goal is to test whether the model can infer and verbalize what the real places are. The team has designed several query types, including country and food queries, and must now decide which real places the hidden identifiers will stand for.
Question: How many and which real cities should serve as the hidden places, and what criteria should guide the choice?
Option 1: Use a small set of five large, well-known cities as the real hidden places that the anonymous city identifiers stand for throughout the Locations fine-tuning task.
Option 2: Use a large set of about one hundred real cities spread across many countries and continents, excluding cities with shared names and balancing for size and cuisine.

Item 5
Context: A research team found that models finetuned on insecure code give broadly misaligned answers to unrelated free-form questions, and that the models describe themselves as highly misaligned. However, in the code experiment the models behave inconsistently across samples: on the same prompt they sometimes act aligned and sometimes misaligned, and on some prompts almost always aligned.
Question: How should the team interpret this inconsistent behavior with respect to whether the model has adopted a coherent misaligned persona?
Option 1: Leave open whether the setup can produce a coherent misaligned persona, noting the behavior is inconsistent across samples but more coherent in code format.
Option 2: Interpret the inconsistency as a misaligned persona that is active only some of the time, and characterize the finetuned model as having adopted that persona.

Item 6
Context: A research team reported expert human scores on benchmark tasks as a baseline. Raters worked in evaluation sessions of fixed length, between 30 minutes and two hours, and were not equally calibrated across tasks. Mean rater scores were often well below the best rater's score on a task.
Question: How strongly should the team state what the reported expert scores represent, given the session time limits on the evaluators?
Option 1: State that the expert scores are strong lower bounds on the human maximum, since an expert with unlimited time could probably score perfectly on every task.
Option 2: Present the mean expert score as the human performance level on each task and treat the best rater score as the human ceiling when claiming models match or beat people.

Item 7
Context: A research team is finetuning a language model to express its uncertainty about arithmetic answers in words rather than numbers. The model is trained on arithmetic questions with target probabilities of being correct. They need a fixed set of words for the model to output as confidence levels during supervised finetuning.
Question: Which set of words should the team use to express confidence levels, and how should they choose it?
Option 1: Use a fixed set of five plain English words ranging from lowest to highest confidence, such as unlikely, doubtful, possible, likely, and certain, chosen by hand.
Option 2: Use five random first names with no inherent ordering as the confidence words the model outputs in supervised finetuning, instead of words ordered from low to high confidence.

Item 8
Context: A research team built a dataset of real forecasting questions with a large news corpus and trained language models to forecast by retrieving articles. They compared model and crowd forecasts and plotted prediction score against how close the question's resolution date was. Both the crowd and an ensemble of the two largest temporal models showed scores that rose as the resolution date got nearer.
Question: How should the team interpret the improvement in prediction scores as the resolution date approaches?
Option 1: Offer a tentative explanation that more relevant information becomes available over time and the model retrieves it from the news corpus, without claiming it as established.
Option 2: Treat the rise as partly reflecting easier questions near resolution, and check by comparing scores on the same questions at fixed retrieval horizons with the crowd.

Item 9
Context: A researcher tried an intervention on a language model and it did not work as expected. They are about to discuss this with a mentor, who will probably ask why it failed and whether the setup was sound. The researcher has time to prepare extra material beforehand.
Question: What evidence should the researcher prepare in advance to answer the mentor's likely questions about the failed intervention?
Option 1: Prepare a few sampled outputs from the intervened model and one hypothesis for the failure, and present them as the likely explanation without any further runs.
Option 2: Prepare backup slides with a data-scaling plot comparing a small and a large training set size to show that adding more data does not fix the failed intervention.

Item 10
Context: A team built a large, diverse benchmark for language models containing both simple JSON tasks and programmatic tasks. Programmatic tasks can involve many sequential model calls and are hard to adapt to some evaluation pipelines, so a full evaluation is computationally expensive. The team wanted others to be able to evaluate models on the benchmark more cheaply.
Question: How should the team provide a cheaper way to evaluate models on the benchmark while keeping it representative?
Option 1: Select a small lightweight subset made up only of simple JSON tasks, chosen to cover the task keywords and to include types such as code, non-English and bias measurement.
Option 2: Release a smaller subset chosen by stratified sampling across task types and difficulty, and verify that model rankings on the subset match rankings on the full benchmark.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
